The two urban centers, Ribeira Grande and Praia, accommodated more than half the entire population of the island (cf. HGCV I 1991: 230–236), with 708 vizinhos (‘households’) and around 6,700 slaves living in them.

In Santiago there is some geographic variation, the north-western region of Santa Caterina being considered the most conservative, and much social and register variation is found in Praia between basilectal and more Portuguese-influenced varieties of the educated people, who, due to professional reasons, speak much Portuguese.
Another 250,000 speakers of Santiago Creole live in diaspora communities around the Atlantic Ocean, mainly in the USA (Boston), São Tomé and Príncipe, Portugal, Angola, Senegal, and the Netherlands.
Some of these emancipated slaves left for other islands (Brava, Santo Antão, São Nicolau) in search of land that could support them.
